Client: Mrs. Lakshmi Devi. Matter: motor accident claim, death of spouse.

Her husband was killed in a road accident involving a commercial truck. The truck driver was operating the vehicle without a valid driving licence. National Insurance Co. denies the claim, arguing the policy is void because the driver was unlicensed, and that it bears no liability.

Key facts: deceased aged 42; monthly income Rs 35,000; dependants are the wife and two minor children (8 and 12); the truck was a commercial vehicle owned by a transport company; the driver held no valid licence; the insurer contests liability.

Research the corpus and advise on supporting precedents, adverse precedents, and strategy.

insurer who otherwise has no liability to pay any amount to the insured but for the
provisions contained in Chapter XI of the Act. This means, the insurer has to pay to

the purpose of promoting the business of the insurance company but to protect the
members of the community who become suffers on account of accidents arising from

payload.holding: The tribunal held that the petitioner is entitled to a total compensation of Rs. 5,74,000 with 9% interest per annum from the date of filing of the petition till realization, payable by the respondent.
payload.ratio: In motor accident claim cases involving the death of a child with no specific proof of actual earnings, compensation towards loss to estate is determined by taking inflation-corrected notional income based on the Second Schedule of the Motor Vehicles Act, applying appropriate personal expense deductions and age-specific multipliers, and adding a similar amount towards composite non-pecuniary damages.

payload.title: Surendra Singh And Another vs Vijay Singh And Another
payload.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
payload.holding: The Court held that the multiplier must be applied with reference to the age of the deceased, future prospects must be awarded even for fixed/self-employed income based on standardized percentages, and the Court has the power under Order XLI Rule 33 CPC to correct and enhance compensation to ensure a just award even if the claimants did not file a cross-appeal.
payload.ratio: In motor accident compensation claims under Section 166 of the MV Act, the multiplier must be selected based on the age of the deceased rather than the claimants, future prospects apply to fixed-salary and self-employed individuals, and appellate courts are obligated under Order XLI Rule 33 and the concept of just compensation to correct and enhance inadequate awards.

Applying the degree test, the Supreme Court has first held that even in the cases of death of a person
in a motor accident who was either self-employed or was working on a fixed salary, an addition (to
loss of income) has to be made towards future prospects. Second, it has been held that
compensation on account of future prospects in such case may be computed at the rate of 40% of the
established income in case of the age of the deceased being below 40 years; at the rate of 25% of the
established income in the case of the age of the deceased between 40 to 50 years and at the rate of
10% in case of age of the deceased being between 50 to 60 years.
The term established income has also been clarified to mean the income minus the tax component.
Question and occasion to examine tax payability arises only if there is a real income. Therefore,
clearly, claim for future prospects would arise only in cases where the claimants are successful in
establishing any amount of definite income earned by the deceased. As a corollary to that, future
prospects may not be awarded in cases of notional income as such income can never be categorised
as established income, it having never been actually and factually earned and it being not real.

payload.holding: The court held that a legal representative who was not dependent upon the deceased at the time of death is not entitled to compensation under the head 'loss of dependency', reducing the total compensation accordingly.

This assertion of the learned Counsel is borne out by the judgment cited by him.
58. In Ram Phal v. Krishna Makkar 1989 ACJ 1126 (P&H), the Punjab and Haryana High Court
considered a case where the licence of the driver of the offending vehicle had expired before the
accident and was renewed nearly after two years of the accident and repelling the contention of the
insurance company that it be absolved of its liability, it was held that insurance company is liable to
pay the compensation as the breach of condition of the policy had not been proved.
59. In National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Abha Sinha 1999 ACJ 450 (Patna), an identical question had
come up for consideration of Patna High Court. In the said case, the period of licence of the driver of
the offending vehicle had expired before the date of accident and it had been renewed covering the
date of accident. The High Court did not accept the contention of the insurance company that it was
absolved of its liability as the driver did not hold a valid driving licence on the date of accident and
observed as follows:

infringement or violation of the promise that the expression 'breach' carries within

itself induces an inference that the violation or infringement on the part of the

and has not done anything he should not have done or is not amiss in any respect

company that the breach was on the part of the insured and that it was the insured
who was guilty of violating the promise or infringement of the contract. Unless the
insured is at fault and is guilty of a breach the insurer cannot escape from the
obligation to indemnify the insured and successfully contend that it is exonerated
having regard to the fact that the promisor (the insured) committed a breach of his

40. It is the contention of the insurance company in both the claim petition Nos. 177 of 1997 and 140
of 1994 that the person who was driving the vehicle at the time of the accident was not holding an
effective driving licence on the date of the accident and, therefore, there is breach of conditions of
the policy requiring that the vehicles shall not be permitted to be driven by a person who does not
hold an effective driving licence. The copy of the insurance certificate issued by the insurer in M.V.C.
No. 177 of 1997 has been marked as Exh. P-6 and the relevant condition regarding the classes of
persons entitled to drive, reads as follows:
Any person including insured provided that a person driving holds an effective
driving licence at the time of the accident and is not disqualified from holding or
obtaining such a licence.

provisions of Chapters X and XI of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. The copy of the insurance policy
has not been produced in M.V.C. No. 177 of 1997. In M.V.C. No. 140 of 1994 the insurance company
has produced Exh.

out any wilful breach.
50. The insurers in both cases have failed to establish before the Tribunal that there was a wilful
breach of the condition of the policy and that the insured had placed the vehicle in the hands of a
person who did not hold an effective driving licence on the date of accident. Even otherwise, the
documents that are produced by the insurance company in these two cases show that drivers of
vehicles in both the cases had driving licences for driving the type of the vehicle which they were
driving on the date of the accident. However, it is the case of the insurance company that the licence
which the respective driver possessed had not been renewed on the date of the accident and it has
been renewed subsequently.
51. The question is as to whether the proof of the fact that on the date of accident in both the cases
the drivers who were holding valid driving licence which had expired had not got renewed their
driving licence on the date of accident and got it renewed subsequently can be said to be proving
that the vehicles were driven by persons who did not possess effective driving licences. In the
present cases, the drivers who had not got their licences renewed on the date of accident do not
stand on the same footing as the persons who did not have any licence at all or the persons who had

were disqualified from obtaining or holding driving licence. The very fact that the licence has been
renewed subsequent to the date of the accident by the drivers in both the cases would show that they
were not disqualified from obtaining driving licence and it is not the case of the insurance company

in both the cases did possess valid driving licence for driving the type of vehicle which they were
driving on the date of accident, but the licences having expired they had not been got renewed
immediately, but got the licence renewed after the date of the accident.

args.question: Motor accident claim by Mrs. Lakshmi Devi (widow) for death of her husband aged 42, monthly income Rs 35,000, with two minor children (8 and 12). Commercial truck accident; driver had no valid driving licence. National Insurance Co. denies liability arguing policy void due to unlicensed driver. Research supporting precedents, adverse precedents, and strategy.

supporting.title: S. Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co. Ltd. & Anr
supporting.principle: An insurer cannot disown its statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties under Section 149 MV Act merely because the driver lacked a specific endorsement to drive a commercial vehicle. The third party's right to recover from the insurer is statutory and paramount.
supporting.fact_alignment: Like our case, involved a commercial vehicle (Mahindra Maxi Cab) where the driver held an LMV licence but lacked a commercial endorsement. The Supreme Court held the insurer liable to the third-party claimant despite the licence defect.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest Supreme Court authority for the proposition that even where the driver's licence is defective for a commercial vehicle, the insurer must pay the third-party claimant. It directly counters the insurer's argument that the policy is 'void'.
supporting.quote: In any case, it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer. It is for the insurer to proceed against the insured for recovery of the amount in the event there has been violation of any condition of the insurance policy.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer has a statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties even if there is a breach of policy conditions (such as an invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover the same from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Directly on point: the court held that even where the driver's licence is invalid, the insurer must satisfy the third-party award and then recover from the owner. Our client is a third-party claimant (wife and children of deceased).
supporting.why_it_matters: This judgment consolidates the entire line of Supreme Court authority (Skandia, Sohan Lal Passi, Kamla, Lehru, Swaran Singh) and confirms that the 'pay and recover' principle applies to all third-party claims regardless of licence defects.
supporting.quote: The insurer who is made statutorily liable to pay compensation to third parties on account of the certificate of insurance issued shall be entitled to recover from the insured the amount paid to the third parties, if there was any breach of policy conditions on account of the vehicle being driven without a valid driving licence.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy, but the insurer must still pay the third-party claimant first and then recover from the owner under the 'pay and recover' principle.
supporting.fact_alignment: Factually closest to our case: the driver had no driving licence at all (not merely expired or wrong class). The tribunal held the breach was fundamental but still ordered pay-and-recover in favour of the third-party claimant.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the most factually analogous case — driver with no licence at all. It confirms that even in the strongest breach scenario, the third-party claimant is protected and the insurer must pay first.
supporting.quote: Though the respondent No.2 insurance company has proved its defence... and as such insurance company is not liable to pay the compensation... but, on the said ground, the petitioner is third party, cannot be made to suffer due to fault of owner... it is proper to direct the respondent No.2 to pay the compensation by reserving liberty to recover the same from the respondent No.1.

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: In third-party motor accident claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific heavy vehicle class, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and may recover the amount from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: Involved a heavy goods vehicle where the driver had only an LMV/transport endorsement. The court applied the pay-and-recover principle. Our case involves a commercial truck — analogous vehicle class issue.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces that the pay-and-recover principle applies across vehicle classes and licence deficiencies in third-party claims.
supporting.quote: The insurer cannot disown its liability on the ground that although the driver was holding a licence to drive a light motor vehicle but before driving light motor vehicle used as commercial vehicle, no endorsement to drive commercial vehicle was obtained.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V. Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only an LMV licence without the specific authorisation required to drive a transport vehicle, the insurer must pay the third-party compensation first and subsequently recover from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver had LMV licence but lacked transport vehicle badge/authorisation. The court ordered pay-and-recover. Our case involves a commercial truck driver with no licence at all — a stronger breach, but the same third-party protection principle applies.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even where the insurer successfully proves breach, the third-party claimant is not left remediless.
supporting.quote: Keeping in view the nature of injuries... the only just and reasonable course would be to direct the Insurance Company to pay compensation to the Claimant and recover it from the owner for his breach of the policy conditions.

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy a third-party award regardless of policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence; non-renewal does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer.
supporting.fact_alignment: Involved expired licences (not no licence at all), but the ratio on statutory third-party protection is directly applicable. The court held the insurer must pay and can recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that the insurer bears the burden of proving wilful breach by the insured — mere absence of a valid licence is not enough to avoid third-party liability.
supporting.quote: The insurer will have to establish that the insured is guilty of an infringement or violation of a promise... The very concept of 'breach' induces an inference that the violation must be a wilful infringement.

supporting.title: Surendra Singh And Another vs Vijay Singh And Another
supporting.principle: Multiplier must be based on deceased's age (not claimants'), future prospects apply to self-employed persons at 25% for age 40-50, and deduction is 1/3rd for 2-3 dependants.
supporting.fact_alignment: Deceased aged 42, self-employed, 3 dependants (wife + 2 minor children). This case directly governs the quantum computation.
supporting.why_it_matters: Provides the authoritative framework for computing compensation: multiplier of 14 (age 42), future prospects at 25% (self-employed, age 40-50), 1/3rd deduction for personal expenses.
supporting.quote: Future prospects have to be included in the loss of income to determine the loss of dependency for award of compensation... 25% of the established income in case of the age of the deceased between 40 to 50 years.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: Where a driver lacks a mandatory special endorsement on the licence, the insurer cannot escape liability to pay compensation to claimants but has the right to recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Involved a tanker carrying hazardous goods where the driver lacked a special endorsement. The court ordered pay-and-recover. Supports the principle that licence deficiencies do not defeat third-party claims.
supporting.why_it_matters: Further reinforces the consistent line of authority that third-party claimants are protected regardless of licence defects.
supporting.quote: The insurance company cannot escape its liability to make payment of compensation awarded in favour of the claimants. Once the payment is made, the insurance company has right to recover the same from the insured.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: The decision in Swaran Singh applies exclusively to third-party risks and does not extend to own-damage claims. A fake driving licence cannot be cured by subsequent renewal.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this to argue that Swaran Singh's liberal approach is limited to third-party risks, and that where the breach is fundamental (no licence at all), the insurer should be completely absolved. They may try to analogise 'no licence' to 'fake licence' and argue the policy is void ab initio.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case expressly affirms at para 41(3) that 'in case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.' Our client is a third-party claimant, not an owner seeking own-damage coverage. The case actually supports our position on third-party claims. The insurer's attempt to use it against us would be a misreading.
adverse.quote: In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co. Ltd. vs Sukumarbai Suryakant Nikam And Ors
adverse.principle: Where a risk is not covered by the policy at all (gratuitous passenger in private vehicle for hire), the Tribunal cannot order 'pay and recover' and the insurer is completely exonerated.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will argue by analogy that driving without any licence is an 'uncovered risk' — like a passenger whose risk is not covered — and therefore the pay-and-recover principle should not apply. They will argue the policy is void for an unlicensed driver, not merely breached.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is fundamentally different. It deals with the scope of risk coverage under Section 147 — whether a particular class of person (gratuitous passenger) is covered at all. Our case is about a breach of policy conditions (licence condition), not about whether the risk of third-party death is covered. Third-party death is always a covered risk under an Act policy. The breach of the licence condition triggers Section 149(2) defences, not a complete absence of coverage.
adverse.quote: Where the passenger travelling from the vehicle for hire or reward, against the policy condition, cannot be treated as 'third party'; then the Tribunal ought not to have passed the order of 'pay and recover'.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co. Ltd vs Minor Mahesh Kanubhai & 2
adverse.principle: Where a risk is neither statutorily required to be covered nor covered under the policy (gratuitous passengers in goods vehicle), the Tribunal has no power to direct pay-and-recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: Similar to doc_028 — the insurer will argue that driving without any licence is a risk so fundamental that it was never intended to be covered, and therefore pay-and-recover is unavailable.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Same distinction as doc_028. The risk of third-party death is statutorily required to be covered under Section 147. The licence condition is a policy term, not a coverage exclusion. The Supreme Court in Swaran Singh and subsequent cases has consistently held that even fundamental breaches of licence conditions do not defeat third-party claims — the insurer must pay and recover.
adverse.quote: In cases where a risk is neither statutorily required to be covered nor covered under the terms of the insurance policy... the provisions of sub-sections (4) and (5) of Section 149 are not attracted.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd. vs Harpreet Singh And Ors.
adverse.principle: Only legal representatives who were dependent upon the deceased at the time of death are entitled to compensation under 'loss of dependency'; non-dependent LRs can only claim loss to estate.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may argue that if any of the three claimants (wife, children aged 8 and 12) are not factually dependent, their claim under loss of dependency should be reduced. However, on these facts, all three are clearly dependent.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: On our facts, the wife and two minor children (aged 8 and 12) are all clearly dependent on the deceased. There is no non-dependent claimant. This case actually supports our position by confirming that genuine dependants are entitled to full loss of dependency compensation.
adverse.quote: A legal representative of a victim of a motor accident, who was not dependent upon the deceased, though can lay a claim for compensation, he is not entitled to compensation under the head 'loss of dependency'.

adverse.title: Liyakat Ali vs Smt Chunni Devi
adverse.principle: Where a vehicle is used for a purpose not covered by the insurance policy (non-agricultural use of a tractor), the insurer is absolved from liability.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this for the broad proposition that fundamental breach of policy conditions can completely absolve the insurer. However, the case is about use of vehicle for a different purpose (non-agricultural), not about driver licence.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is about a use-based exclusion (agricultural vs non-agricultural use), not about driver licence conditions. The line of authority on licence breaches (Swaran Singh, Iyyapan, Satto) consistently applies pay-and-recover for third-party claims. Use-based exclusions are different from driver competence conditions.
adverse.quote: The tractor was insured only for the purpose of agricultural activity... Transportation of iron rods and bricks is certainly not an agricultural activity... there is a violation of the terms and conditions of the insurance policy.

adverse.title: Shivlal And Ors. vs Smt. Rukmabai And Ors.
adverse.principle: The insurer is not liable for the death of a gratuitous passenger in a goods vehicle whose risk is not statutorily required to be covered.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that certain risks are simply not covered and the insurer cannot be held liable. However, this is about passenger coverage, not driver licence.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case concerns gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles — a category of persons whose risk is not statutorily required to be covered under Section 147. Our case involves a third-party road user (the deceased was not in the truck but was killed by it). Third-party road users are always covered under an Act policy. The case is entirely distinguishable.
adverse.quote: The insurer is not liable to pay compensation for the death of a gratuitous passenger carried in a goods vehicle.

priority_arguments: 1. The insurer's primary defence — that the policy is 'void' because the driver had no licence — is legally unsustainable. Under the consistent line of Supreme Court authority (S. Iyyapan, Satto, Swaran Singh), the insurer's statutory liability to third parties under Section 149 MV Act is independent of policy conditions. The insurer must pay the claimant and may then recover from the insured owner.

2. The 'pay and recover' principle applies with full force. Even where the breach is fundamental (no licence at all, as in Sunil Shreesail Killiket), the third-party claimant cannot be made to suffer. The insurer must satisfy the award in the first instance.

3. On quantum: the deceased was 42 years old, self-employed, with monthly income of Rs 35,000. Applying Sarla Verma / Pranay Sethi framework: future prospects at 25% (age 40-50, self-employed), multiplier of 14, 1/3rd deduction for personal expenses (3 dependants). Conventional heads as per Pranay Sethi and Magma General.

4. The burden of proving wilful breach by the insured (owner/transport company) lies on the insurer under Section 149(2). Mere absence of a licence does not automatically absolve the insurer — they must show the owner knowingly permitted an unlicensed driver (K.G. Srinivasamurthy).
strategy.compensation_range: Rs 50,99,650 to Rs 52,95,650 (approximately Rs 51-53 lakhs) plus interest at 7.5-9% p.a. from the date of the claim petition.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: Computed using the compute_quantum tool: Monthly income Rs 35,000 → Annual Rs 4,20,000. Add 25% future prospects (self-employed, age 42) = Rs 5,25,000. Deduct 1/3rd for personal expenses (3 dependants: wife + 2 minor children) = Rs 3,50,000. Apply multiplier 14 (age 42) = Rs 49,00,000. Add conventional heads: loss of estate Rs 19,965 + funeral Rs 19,965 + spousal consortium Rs 79,860 + parental consortium for 2 children Rs 79,860 = Rs 1,99,650. Total: Rs 50,99,650. The range reflects potential variation if the tribunal treats the deceased as having 'permanent employment' (50% future prospects) instead of self-employed (25%).
risks: 1. The insurer may argue that 'no licence at all' is a more fundamental breach than 'wrong class of licence' or 'expired licence', and seek complete exoneration. However, Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024) directly addresses this — even with no licence, pay-and-recover applies.

2. The insurer may attempt to argue that the owner/transport company knowingly employed an unlicensed driver, constituting a wilful breach. This actually helps the claimant — it confirms the breach is on the owner's part, not the claimant's, and the insurer must still pay the third party.

3. The insurer may challenge the income proof (Rs 35,000/month). Ensure documentary evidence of income (salary slips, bank statements, IT returns) is robust. If income is not fully proved, the tribunal may fall back on notional income, reducing the award.
4. The insurer may argue contributory negligence if the deceased contributed to the accident. Check the FIR and police report. If no contributory negligence is alleged, this risk is minimal.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: File claim under Section 166 MV Act before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal having jurisdiction over the place of accident. Seek the full computed compensation of Rs 51-53 lakhs. Argue for pay-and-recover against the insurer in the first instance. The owner/transport company should be joined as a co-respondent. If the insurer persists in denying liability, seek a specific direction under Section 149(4)/(5) for pay-and-recover, supported by the consistent line of Supreme Court and High Court authorities cited above.

caveats: The corpus does not contain any judgment where the insurer was completely absolved from third-party liability solely on the ground that the driver had no licence. Every judgment in this corpus that addresses a licence defect in a third-party claim applies the pay-and-recover principle. This is consistent with the settled legal position under Swaran Singh and subsequent authorities.

The quantum computation assumes the deceased was self-employed. If evidence shows permanent employment, future prospects increase to 50% (for age under 40) or 30% (for age 40-50), which would increase the award.

The conventional heads figures (Rs 19,965 for loss of estate and funeral, Rs 79,860 for consortium per claimant) are based on the Pranay Sethi framework as updated for inflation. The tribunal may apply slightly different figures depending on the year of the award.

No judgment in the corpus addresses the specific scenario of a commercial truck owned by a transport company where the company knowingly employed an unlicensed driver. This factual nuance may affect the tribunal's view on whether the breach was 'wilful' on the owner's part, but does not affect the third-party claimant's right to recover from the insurer.

payload.court: In The High Court Of Karnataka At Bengaluru
payload.holding: The Court held that where a driving license is renewed more than 30 days after its expiry, it takes effect from the date of renewal and does not cover the interregnum period of the accident, but directed the insurance company to satisfy the award and recover the amount from the insured owner under the 'pay and recover' principle.
payload.ratio: When an application for renewal of a driving license is made more than 30 days after its expiry, the license is renewed from the date of renewal; thus, the driver does not hold a valid license on the date of an accident occurring during the lapsed period, absolving the insurer of primary liability, though a 'pay and recover' order may be issued in favour of third-party claimants.

finding, which is based on correct and proper appraisal of the evidence makes the maxim of res ipsa
loquitur applicable to the facts of the present case because the things are so apparent that the
question of contributory negligence does not arise. The plea of contributory negligence can be raised
only, where both the parties were in some respects negligent, when there are the findings in
unambiguous and clear terms that the deceased was hit by the jeep from behind, then no question of

only, where both the parties were in some respects negligent, when there are the findings in

contributory negligence on the part of the deceased arises and the things being obvious, apparent '
and self-speaking, there was no question of any contributory negligence on the part of the deceased.
It is true that no specific finding has been recorded by the learned Tribunal on the plea of the
contributory negligence but as said above, the facts being clear and self-speaking, there was no need
to consider such a plea which was evidently unsustainable and not recording any finding thereon

args.question: Motor accident claim by Mrs. Lakshmi Devi (widow) for death of her husband aged 42, monthly income Rs 35,000, with two minor children (8 and 12). Commercial truck accident; driver had no valid driving licence. National Insurance Co. denies liability arguing policy void due to unlicensed driver. Research supporting precedents, adverse precedents, and strategy.

supporting.title: S. Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co. Ltd. & Anr
supporting.principle: An insurer cannot disown its statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties under Section 149 MV Act merely because the driver lacked a specific endorsement to drive a commercial vehicle. The third party's right to recover from the insurer is statutory and paramount.
supporting.fact_alignment: Like our case, involved a commercial vehicle (Mahindra Maxi Cab) where the driver held an LMV licence but lacked a commercial endorsement. The Supreme Court held the insurer liable to the third-party claimant despite the licence defect.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest Supreme Court authority for the proposition that even where the driver's licence is defective for a commercial vehicle, the insurer must pay the third-party claimant. It directly counters the insurer's argument that the policy is 'void'.
supporting.quote: In any case, it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer. It is for the insurer to proceed against the insured for recovery of the amount in the event there has been violation of any condition of the insurance policy.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer has a statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties even if there is a breach of policy conditions (such as an invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover the same from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Directly on point: the court held that even where the driver's licence is invalid, the insurer must satisfy the third-party award and then recover from the owner. Our client is a third-party claimant (wife and children of deceased).
supporting.why_it_matters: This judgment consolidates the entire line of Supreme Court authority (Skandia, Sohan Lal Passi, Kamla, Lehru, Swaran Singh) and confirms that the 'pay and recover' principle applies to all third-party claims regardless of licence defects.
supporting.quote: The insurer who is made statutorily liable to pay compensation to third parties on account of the certificate of insurance issued shall be entitled to recover from the insured the amount paid to the third parties, if there was any breach of policy conditions on account of the vehicle being driven without a valid driving licence.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy, but the insurer must still pay the third-party claimant first and then recover from the owner under the 'pay and recover' principle.
supporting.fact_alignment: Factually closest to our case: the driver had no driving licence at all (not merely expired or wrong class). The tribunal held the breach was fundamental but still ordered pay-and-recover in favour of the third-party claimant.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the most factually analogous case — driver with no licence at all. It confirms that even in the strongest breach scenario, the third-party claimant is protected and the insurer must pay first.
supporting.quote: Though the respondent No.2 insurance company has proved its defence... and as such insurance company is not liable to pay the compensation... but, on the said ground, the petitioner is third party, cannot be made to suffer due to fault of owner... it is proper to direct the respondent No.2 to pay the compensation by reserving liberty to recover the same from the respondent No.1.

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: In third-party motor accident claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific heavy vehicle class, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and may recover the amount from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: Involved a heavy goods vehicle where the driver had only an LMV/transport endorsement. The court applied the pay-and-recover principle. Our case involves a commercial truck — analogous vehicle class issue.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces that the pay-and-recover principle applies across vehicle classes and licence deficiencies in third-party claims.
supporting.quote: The insurer cannot disown its liability on the ground that although the driver was holding a licence to drive a light motor vehicle but before driving light motor vehicle used as commercial vehicle, no endorsement to drive commercial vehicle was obtained.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V. Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only an LMV licence without the specific authorisation required to drive a transport vehicle, the insurer must pay the third-party compensation first and subsequently recover from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver had LMV licence but lacked transport vehicle badge/authorisation. The court ordered pay-and-recover. Our case involves a commercial truck driver with no licence at all — a stronger breach, but the same third-party protection principle applies.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even where the insurer successfully proves breach, the third-party claimant is not left remediless.
supporting.quote: Keeping in view the nature of injuries... the only just and reasonable course would be to direct the Insurance Company to pay compensation to the Claimant and recover it from the owner for his breach of the policy conditions.

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy a third-party award regardless of policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence; non-renewal does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer.
supporting.fact_alignment: Involved expired licences (not no licence at all), but the ratio on statutory third-party protection is directly applicable. The court held the insurer must pay and can recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that the insurer bears the burden of proving wilful breach by the insured — mere absence of a valid licence is not enough to avoid third-party liability.
supporting.quote: The insurer will have to establish that the insured is guilty of an infringement or violation of a promise... The very concept of 'breach' induces an inference that the violation must be a wilful infringement.

supporting.title: Surendra Singh And Another vs Vijay Singh And Another
supporting.principle: Multiplier must be based on deceased's age (not claimants'), future prospects apply to self-employed persons at 25% for age 40-50, and deduction is 1/3rd for 2-3 dependants.
supporting.fact_alignment: Deceased aged 42, self-employed, 3 dependants (wife + 2 minor children). This case directly governs the quantum computation.
supporting.why_it_matters: Provides the authoritative framework for computing compensation: multiplier of 14 (age 42), future prospects at 25% (self-employed, age 40-50), 1/3rd deduction for personal expenses.
supporting.quote: Future prospects have to be included in the loss of income to determine the loss of dependency for award of compensation... 25% of the established income in case of the age of the deceased between 40 to 50 years.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: Where a driver lacks a mandatory special endorsement on the licence, the insurer cannot escape liability to pay compensation to claimants but has the right to recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Involved a tanker carrying hazardous goods where the driver lacked a special endorsement. The court ordered pay-and-recover. Supports the principle that licence deficiencies do not defeat third-party claims.
supporting.why_it_matters: Further reinforces the consistent line of authority that third-party claimants are protected regardless of licence defects.
supporting.quote: The insurance company cannot escape its liability to make payment of compensation awarded in favour of the claimants. Once the payment is made, the insurance company has right to recover the same from the insured.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar
supporting.principle: Where a driving licence is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, it takes effect from the date of renewal and does not cover the interregnum; however, the insurer must still satisfy the third-party award and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver's licence had expired and was renewed after the accident. The court held the driver had no valid licence on the accident date but still ordered pay-and-recover in favour of the third-party claimants.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even where the insurer proves the driver had no effective licence on the accident date, the third-party claimant is protected by the pay-and-recover principle.
supporting.quote: Since it is the statutory right of the third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded either from the owner or the driver, as the vehicle in question is insured, the insurance company shall pay the amount and recover the same from driver or the insured.

supporting.title: National Insurance Company Ltd vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
supporting.principle: Even where the driver lacks a valid driving licence, the insurer remains liable to satisfy third-party claims subject to a right of recovery from the vehicle owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The insurer's appeal was dismissed; the court upheld the pay-and-recover order despite the driver having no valid licence. The court also set aside a finding of contributory negligence against the deceased.
supporting.why_it_matters: Directly supports our position: the insurer's appeal against pay-and-recover was rejected. Also shows that courts are reluctant to find contributory negligence against the deceased without clear evidence.
supporting.quote: Learned Tribunal though has accepted that there was no valid licence with the driver of the Tanker but even then has directed the insurance company to pay compensation to the claimants with a right to recover it from the owner.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: The decision in Swaran Singh applies exclusively to third-party risks and does not extend to own-damage claims. A fake driving licence cannot be cured by subsequent renewal.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this to argue that Swaran Singh's liberal approach is limited to third-party risks, and that where the breach is fundamental (no licence at all), the insurer should be completely absolved. They may try to analogise 'no licence' to 'fake licence' and argue the policy is void ab initio.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case expressly affirms at para 41(3) that 'in case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.' Our client is a third-party claimant, not an owner seeking own-damage coverage. The case actually supports our position on third-party claims. The insurer's attempt to use it against us would be a misreading.
adverse.quote: In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co. Ltd. vs Sukumarbai Suryakant Nikam And Ors
adverse.principle: Where a risk is not covered by the policy at all (gratuitous passenger in private vehicle for hire), the Tribunal cannot order 'pay and recover' and the insurer is completely exonerated.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will argue by analogy that driving without any licence is an 'uncovered risk' — like a passenger whose risk is not covered — and therefore the pay-and-recover principle should not apply. They will argue the policy is void for an unlicensed driver, not merely breached.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is fundamentally different. It deals with the scope of risk coverage under Section 147 — whether a particular class of person (gratuitous passenger) is covered at all. Our case is about a breach of policy conditions (licence condition), not about whether the risk of third-party death is covered. Third-party death is always a covered risk under an Act policy. The breach of the licence condition triggers Section 149(2) defences, not a complete absence of coverage.
adverse.quote: Where the passenger travelling from the vehicle for hire or reward, against the policy condition, cannot be treated as 'third party'; then the Tribunal ought not to have passed the order of 'pay and recover'.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co. Ltd vs Minor Mahesh Kanubhai & 2
adverse.principle: Where a risk is neither statutorily required to be covered nor covered under the policy (gratuitous passengers in goods vehicle), the Tribunal has no power to direct pay-and-recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: Similar to doc_028 — the insurer will argue that driving without any licence is a risk so fundamental that it was never intended to be covered, and therefore pay-and-recover is unavailable.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Same distinction as doc_028. The risk of third-party death is statutorily required to be covered under Section 147. The licence condition is a policy term, not a coverage exclusion. The Supreme Court in Swaran Singh and subsequent cases has consistently held that even fundamental breaches of licence conditions do not defeat third-party claims — the insurer must pay and recover.
adverse.quote: In cases where a risk is neither statutorily required to be covered nor covered under the terms of the insurance policy... the provisions of sub-sections (4) and (5) of Section 149 are not attracted.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd. vs Harpreet Singh And Ors.
adverse.principle: Only legal representatives who were dependent upon the deceased at the time of death are entitled to compensation under 'loss of dependency'; non-dependent LRs can only claim loss to estate.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may argue that if any of the three claimants (wife, children aged 8 and 12) are not factually dependent, their claim under loss of dependency should be reduced. However, on these facts, all three are clearly dependent.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: On our facts, the wife and two minor children (aged 8 and 12) are all clearly dependent on the deceased. There is no non-dependent claimant. This case actually supports our position by confirming that genuine dependants are entitled to full loss of dependency compensation.
adverse.quote: A legal representative of a victim of a motor accident, who was not dependent upon the deceased, though can lay a claim for compensation, he is not entitled to compensation under the head 'loss of dependency'.

adverse.title: Kamal S/O Shiv Ram vs Mursleem S/O Mohd. Akil
adverse.principle: Contributory negligence can be inferred when the injured rider is proven to have been driving without a valid driving licence and without wearing a helmet.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that driving without a licence is itself evidence of contributory negligence. However, this case involved the injured claimant himself driving without a licence — not a deceased third party. The deceased in our case was not driving the offending vehicle.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is about contributory negligence of the claimant himself (who was driving without a licence). In our case, the deceased was a third-party road user, not the driver of the offending truck. The absence of the truck driver's licence has no bearing on the deceased's own conduct. The case is entirely distinguishable.
adverse.quote: Contributory negligence is established when the injured rider is proven to have been driving without a valid driving license and without wearing a helmet.

priority_arguments: 1. The insurer's primary defence — that the policy is 'void' because the driver had no licence — is legally unsustainable. Under the consistent line of Supreme Court authority (S. Iyyapan, Satto, Swaran Singh), the insurer's statutory liability to third parties under Section 149 MV Act is independent of policy conditions. The insurer must pay the claimant and may then recover from the insured owner.

2. The 'pay and recover' principle applies with full force. Even where the breach is fundamental (no licence at all, as in Sunil Shreesail Killiket), the third-party claimant cannot be made to suffer. The insurer must satisfy the award in the first instance.

3. On quantum: the deceased was 42 years old, self-employed, with monthly income of Rs 35,000. Applying Sarla Verma / Pranay Sethi framework: future prospects at 25% (age 40-50, self-employed), multiplier of 14, 1/3rd deduction for personal expenses (3 dependants). Conventional heads as per Pranay Sethi and Magma General.

4. The burden of proving wilful breach by the insured (owner/transport company) lies on the insurer under Section 149(2). Mere absence of a licence does not automatically absolve the insurer — they must show the owner knowingly permitted an unlicensed driver (K.G. Srinivasamurthy).

5. If the insurer raises contributory negligence, cite Suman Lata (doc_023) for the principle that res ipsa loquitur applies when a vehicle hits a third party, and Meena (doc_006) for the principle that courts should not infer contributory negligence from assumptions.

result.question: Motor accident claim by Mrs. Lakshmi Devi (widow) for death of her husband aged 42, monthly income Rs 35,000, with two minor children (8 and 12). Commercial truck accident; driver had no valid driving licence. National Insurance Co. denies liability arguing policy void due to unlicensed driver. Research supporting precedents, adverse precedents, and strategy.

supporting.title: S. Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co. Ltd. & Anr
supporting.principle: An insurer cannot disown its statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties under Section 149 MV Act merely because the driver lacked a specific endorsement to drive a commercial vehicle. The third party's right to recover from the insurer is statutory and paramount.
supporting.fact_alignment: Like our case, involved a commercial vehicle (Mahindra Maxi Cab) where the driver held an LMV licence but lacked a commercial endorsement. The Supreme Court held the insurer liable to the third-party claimant despite the licence defect.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest Supreme Court authority for the proposition that even where the driver's licence is defective for a commercial vehicle, the insurer must pay the third-party claimant. It directly counters the insurer's argument that the policy is 'void'.
supporting.quote: In any case, it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer. It is for the insurer to proceed against the insured for recovery of the amount in the event there has been violation of any condition of the insurance policy.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer has a statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties even if there is a breach of policy conditions (such as an invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover the same from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Directly on point: the court held that even where the driver's licence is invalid, the insurer must satisfy the third-party award and then recover from the owner. Our client is a third-party claimant (wife and children of deceased).
supporting.why_it_matters: This judgment consolidates the entire line of Supreme Court authority (Skandia, Sohan Lal Passi, Kamla, Lehru, Swaran Singh) and confirms that the 'pay and recover' principle applies to all third-party claims regardless of licence defects.
supporting.quote: The insurer who is made statutorily liable to pay compensation to third parties on account of the certificate of insurance issued shall be entitled to recover from the insured the amount paid to the third parties, if there was any breach of policy conditions on account of the vehicle being driven without a valid driving licence.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy, but the insurer must still pay the third-party claimant first and then recover from the owner under the 'pay and recover' principle.
supporting.fact_alignment: Factually closest to our case: the driver had no driving licence at all (not merely expired or wrong class). The tribunal held the breach was fundamental but still ordered pay-and-recover in favour of the third-party claimant.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the most factually analogous case — driver with no licence at all. It confirms that even in the strongest breach scenario, the third-party claimant is protected and the insurer must pay first.

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: In third-party motor accident claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific heavy vehicle class, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and may recover the amount from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: Involved a heavy goods vehicle where the driver had only an LMV/transport endorsement. The court applied the pay-and-recover principle. Our case involves a commercial truck — analogous vehicle class issue.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces that the pay-and-recover principle applies across vehicle classes and licence deficiencies in third-party claims.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V. Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only an LMV licence without the specific authorisation required to drive a transport vehicle, the insurer must pay the third-party compensation first and subsequently recover from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver had LMV licence but lacked transport vehicle badge/authorisation. The court ordered pay-and-recover. Our case involves a commercial truck driver with no licence at all — a stronger breach, but the same third-party protection principle applies.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even where the insurer successfully proves breach, the third-party claimant is not left remediless.

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy a third-party award regardless of policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence; non-renewal does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer.
supporting.fact_alignment: Involved expired licences (not no licence at all), but the ratio on statutory third-party protection is directly applicable. The court held the insurer must pay and can recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that the insurer bears the burden of proving wilful breach by the insured — mere absence of a valid licence is not enough to avoid third-party liability.

supporting.title: Surendra Singh And Another vs Vijay Singh And Another
supporting.principle: Multiplier must be based on deceased's age (not claimants'), future prospects apply to self-employed persons at 25% for age 40-50, and deduction is 1/3rd for 2-3 dependants.
supporting.fact_alignment: Deceased aged 42, self-employed, 3 dependants (wife + 2 minor children). This case directly governs the quantum computation.
supporting.why_it_matters: Provides the authoritative framework for computing compensation: multiplier of 14 (age 42), future prospects at 25% (self-employed, age 40-50), 1/3rd deduction for personal expenses.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: Where a driver lacks a mandatory special endorsement on the licence, the insurer cannot escape liability to pay compensation to claimants but has the right to recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Involved a tanker carrying hazardous goods where the driver lacked a special endorsement. The court ordered pay-and-recover. Supports the principle that licence deficiencies do not defeat third-party claims.
supporting.why_it_matters: Further reinforces the consistent line of authority that third-party claimants are protected regardless of licence defects.
supporting.quote: The insurance company cannot escape its liability to make payment of compensation awarded in favour of the claimants. Once the payment is made, the insurance company has right to recover the same from the insured.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar
supporting.principle: Where a driving licence is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, it takes effect from the date of renewal and does not cover the interregnum; however, the insurer must still satisfy the third-party award and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver's licence had expired and was renewed after the accident. The court held the driver had no valid licence on the accident date but still ordered pay-and-recover in favour of the third-party claimants.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even where the insurer proves the driver had no effective licence on the accident date, the third-party claimant is protected by the pay-and-recover principle.
supporting.quote: Since it is the statutory right of the third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded either from the owner or the driver, as the vehicle in question is insured, the insurance company shall pay the amount and recover the same from driver or the insured.

supporting.title: National Insurance Company Ltd vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
supporting.principle: Even where the driver lacks a valid driving licence, the insurer remains liable to satisfy third-party claims subject to a right of recovery from the vehicle owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The insurer's appeal was dismissed; the court upheld the pay-and-recover order despite the driver having no valid licence. The court also set aside a finding of contributory negligence against the deceased.
supporting.why_it_matters: Directly supports our position: the insurer's appeal against pay-and-recover was rejected. Also shows that courts are reluctant to find contributory negligence against the deceased without clear evidence.
supporting.quote: Learned Tribunal though has accepted that there was no valid licence with the driver of the Tanker but even then has directed the insurance company to pay compensation to the claimants with a right to recover it from the owner.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: The decision in Swaran Singh applies exclusively to third-party risks and does not extend to own-damage claims. A fake driving licence cannot be cured by subsequent renewal.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this to argue that Swaran Singh's liberal approach is limited to third-party risks, and that where the breach is fundamental (no licence at all), the insurer should be completely absolved. They may try to analogise 'no licence' to 'fake licence' and argue the policy is void ab initio.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case expressly affirms at para 41(3) that 'in case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.' Our client is a third-party claimant, not an owner seeking own-damage coverage. The case actually supports our position on third-party claims. The insurer's attempt to use it against us would be a misreading.
adverse.quote: In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co. Ltd. vs Sukumarbai Suryakant Nikam And Ors
adverse.principle: Where a risk is not covered by the policy at all (gratuitous passenger in private vehicle for hire), the Tribunal cannot order 'pay and recover' and the insurer is completely exonerated.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will argue by analogy that driving without any licence is an 'uncovered risk' — like a passenger whose risk is not covered — and therefore the pay-and-recover principle should not apply. They will argue the policy is void for an unlicensed driver, not merely breached.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is fundamentally different. It deals with the scope of risk coverage under Section 147 — whether a particular class of person (gratuitous passenger) is covered at all. Our case is about a breach of policy conditions (licence condition), not about whether the risk of third-party death is covered. Third-party death is always a covered risk under an Act policy. The breach of the licence condition triggers Section 149(2) defences, not a complete absence of coverage.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co. Ltd vs Minor Mahesh Kanubhai & 2
adverse.principle: Where a risk is neither statutorily required to be covered nor covered under the policy (gratuitous passengers in goods vehicle), the Tribunal has no power to direct pay-and-recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: Similar to doc_028 — the insurer will argue that driving without any licence is a risk so fundamental that it was never intended to be covered, and therefore pay-and-recover is unavailable.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Same distinction as doc_028. The risk of third-party death is statutorily required to be covered under Section 147. The licence condition is a policy term, not a coverage exclusion. The Supreme Court in Swaran Singh and subsequent cases has consistently held that even fundamental breaches of licence conditions do not defeat third-party claims — the insurer must pay and recover.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd. vs Harpreet Singh And Ors.
adverse.principle: Only legal representatives who were dependent upon the deceased at the time of death are entitled to compensation under 'loss of dependency'; non-dependent LRs can only claim loss to estate.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may argue that if any of the three claimants (wife, children aged 8 and 12) are not factually dependent, their claim under loss of dependency should be reduced. However, on these facts, all three are clearly dependent.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: On our facts, the wife and two minor children (aged 8 and 12) are all clearly dependent on the deceased. There is no non-dependent claimant. This case actually supports our position by confirming that genuine dependants are entitled to full loss of dependency compensation.
adverse.quote: A legal representative of a victim of a motor accident, who was not dependent upon the deceased, though can lay a claim for compensation, he is not entitled to compensation under the head 'loss of dependency'.

adverse.title: Kamal S/O Shiv Ram vs Mursleem S/O Mohd. Akil
adverse.principle: Contributory negligence can be inferred when the injured rider is proven to have been driving without a valid driving licence and without wearing a helmet.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that driving without a licence is itself evidence of contributory negligence. However, this case involved the injured claimant himself driving without a licence — not a deceased third party. The deceased in our case was not driving the offending vehicle.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is about contributory negligence of the claimant himself (who was driving without a licence). In our case, the deceased was a third-party road user, not the driver of the offending truck. The absence of the truck driver's licence has no bearing on the deceased's own conduct. The case is entirely distinguishable.
